lead: An ARM processor can run two instruction sets. ARM instructions are 32 bits wide: they carry a 4-bit condition field, an optional S suffix that updates the flags, and a full choice of operands. Thumb instructions are a 16-bit compressed subset that saves program memory; Thumb-2 mixes 16-bit and 32-bit forms. The same core executes both, so a designer trades code size against instruction choice. You meet this in phones, routers, and microcontroller boards where flash is small but the CPU must still run fast.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for the 16 registers, processor modes and the N,Z,C,V flags in the CPSR.

sections.h3: ARM words, Thumb words, and the condition field

blocks.text: An ARM instruction is one 32-bit word. Bits 31–28 hold the condition field. The core tests the condition against the CPSR flags; if the condition is false, the instruction does nothing. Standard codes: EQ (Z=1), NE (Z=0), CS/HS (C=1), CC/LO (C=0), MI (N=1), PL (N=0), VS (V=1), VC (V=0), HI (C=1 and Z=0), LS (C=0 or Z=1), GE (N=V), LT (N≠V), GT (Z=0 and N=V), LE (Z=1 or N≠V), and AL (always). This lets one compare set the flags and many following instructions run or skip without branches.

The S suffix is one bit in the instruction encoding. Without S the instruction does not change N, Z, C or V. With S it updates them. ADD R0,R1,R2 leaves the flags alone; ADDS R0,R1,R2 sets them from the result. The condition field reads old flags, so the order matters: a compare or an S-form must come before a conditional instruction.

Thumb is not a separate CPU. It is a 16-bit encoding of common ARM operations. A Thumb instruction has less room for a condition field and for large immediates. Thumb-2 keeps 16-bit forms for density and adds 32-bit forms for operations that need more bits. Some syllabi call the older 16-bit set Thumb-1.

sections.h3: Data processing, operands and the barrel shifter

blocks.text: Data processing instructions work on registers. The main mnemonics are AND, EOR, SUB, RSB, ADD, ADC, SBC, RSC, TST, TEQ, CMP, CMN, ORR, MOV, BIC and MVN. ADC adds with carry; SBC subtracts with borrow. RSB reverses the subtraction: RSB R0,R1,R2 computes R2 − R1. TST, TEQ, CMP and CMN only set flags; they do not write a result register.

The second operand can take three forms. An immediate is a constant written with #, for example #5. A register is a plain register, for example R2. A shifted register passes through the barrel shifter before the ALU. The shifter can do LSL (logical shift left), LSR (logical shift right), ASR (arithmetic shift right) and ROR (rotate right) by #n or by a register. ADD R0,R1,R2,LSL #2 computes R0 = R1 + (R2 × 4). The shift is free in the same instruction; it does not need a separate instruction.

After an S-form, the four flags mean this. N is 1 when bit 31 of the result is 1. Z is 1 when the result is zero. C is the carry out of bit 31 for an addition. For a subtraction, C is the inverse of the borrow: C = 1 when the subtraction needs no borrow (unsigned Rn ≥ Rm) and C = 0 when a borrow occurs. Example: CMP R1,R2 with R1 = 5 and R2 = 2 gives C = 1; with R1 = 2 and R2 = 5 it gives C = 0. V is 1 when signed overflow occurs: for an addition, both inputs have the same sign and the result has the other sign. For a subtraction, V is 1 when the operands have different signs and the result has the sign of the second operand (equivalently, differs from the sign of the first operand). These are the same CPSR flags from Chapter 2.3.

sections.h3: Load/store, branch, multiply, status and assembler directives

blocks.text: Load and store instructions move data between registers and memory. LDR loads a 32-bit word; STR stores a 32-bit word. LDRB and STRB move one byte. LDM loads a list of registers from consecutive addresses; STM stores a list. The ! after the base register means writeback: the base register is updated after the transfer. LDM and STM have a rule about the base register. With writeback (!) and the base register also in the list, the value left in the base by LDM, or stored for it by STM, is UNPREDICTABLE or UNKNOWN in the architecture. Correct code keeps the base out of the list.

Branch instructions change the PC. B is a plain branch. BL is branch with link: it copies the return address into LR (R14) before branching, so a subroutine can return with BX LR. BX branches to the address in a register; the low bit of that address selects ARM or Thumb state (it must be 1 on Thumb-only cores such as Cortex-M). Multiply instructions include MUL (R0 = R1 × R2), MLA (multiply and accumulate), UMULL and SMULL (unsigned and signed 64-bit results). Status instructions MRS and MSR move between a general register and the CPSR or SPSR. SWI (software interrupt, called SVC in newer ARM) enters a supervisor call.

items: Keil-style directives are not machine instructions. AREA names a code or data section.
ENTRY marks the first instruction to execute. EXPORT makes a label visible to the linker.
DCD places a 32-bit constant in memory. EQU defines a symbol.
Thumb does not support every ARM instruction or every conditional form. Thumb-2 adds 32-bit forms and IT blocks for conditional execution.

figure.caption: ARM instruction classes. ADDS carries the S suffix and updates the flags; plain ADD leaves them unchanged.

spec.aria: The tree shows three ARM instruction classes: data processing (ADD and the flag-setting ADDS), load/store (LDR and STR), and branch (B and BL).

examples.question: R1 = 0x7FFFFFFF and R2 = 0x00000001. The instruction ADDS R0,R1,R2 executes. Give R0 and the N,Z,C,V flags after it. State why each flag has that value.
steps: Convert the inputs: R1 = 0x7FFFFFFF = 2147483647 and R2 = 0x00000001 = 1.
N is bit 31 of R0. Bit 31 of 0x80000000 is 1, so N = 1.
Z is 1 only when the result is zero. R0 is not zero, so Z = 0.
C is the unsigned carry out of bit 31. The sum 0x7FFFFFFF + 1 fits in 32 bits without a carry beyond bit 31, so C = 0.
V is signed overflow. Two positive inputs produced a negative result, so V = 1. Using signs: R1 and R2 are both positive, R0 has bit 31 = 1 (negative).
examples.check:
r1 = 0x7FFFFFFF
r2 = 0x00000001
s = r1 + r2
r0 = s & 0xFFFFFFFF
N = (r0 >> 31) & 1
Z = 1 if r0 == 0 else 0
C = 1 if s > 0xFFFFFFFF else 0
V = 1 if ((r1 ^ r0) & (r2 ^ r0) & 0x80000000) else 0
print(r1)
print(r2)
print(r0)
print(N)
print(Z)
print(C)
print(V)

traps: Flags change only when the S suffix is present. ADD R0,R1,R2 does not update N,Z,C,V; ADDS does.
Thumb does not support every ARM instruction or every conditional form. Many Thumb instructions are unconditional; Thumb-2 uses IT blocks where a condition is needed.

In LDM and STM with writeback (!), if the base register is also in the register list, the value left in the base (LDM) or stored for it (STM) is UNPREDICTABLE or UNKNOWN in the architecture. Keep the base out of the list.
RSB reverses the subtraction: RSB R0,R1,R2 is R2 − R1, not R1 − R2. This is a common sign slip.
A conditional instruction reads the flags left by an earlier S-form or compare. If the earlier instruction had no S suffix, the condition may test stale flags.

quiz.a: A Thumb instruction is a 16-bit encoding of common ARM operations. It saves program memory compared with a 32-bit ARM instruction.

quiz.q: Why does the ARM instruction set have a condition field?
quiz.a: The 4-bit condition field lets an instruction run only when the CPSR flags match the condition. A compare followed by conditional instructions avoids extra branches.

quiz.q: R4 = 5 and R5 = 2. What does ADD R3,R4,R5,LSL #3 compute?
quiz.a: LSL #3 multiplies R5 by 8: 2 × 8 = 16. Then R3 = R4 + 16 = 5 + 16 = 21.

quiz.q: After CMP R1,R2 the instruction ADDEQ R0,R1,R2 follows. If R1 equals R2, what happens?
quiz.a: CMP subtracts R2 from R1 and sets the flags. Equal operands give a zero result, so Z = 1. The EQ condition is true, so ADDEQ executes and R0 = R1 + R2.

quiz.q: List four data processing mnemonics and one that only sets flags.
quiz.a: Examples of data processing mnemonics: ADD, SUB, AND, MOV, ORR. CMP only sets flags; it does not write a result register.

quiz.q: What does the S suffix do, and what happens without it?
quiz.a: The S suffix makes the instruction update N, Z, C and V from its result. Without S the instruction leaves those flags unchanged.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to put the base register in the register list of STM with writeback?
quiz.a: Writeback and the list both touch the base register. With writeback (!) and the base also in the list, the value stored for the base is UNKNOWN in the architecture, so the saved value is not a defined one. Keeping the base out of the list avoids this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern ARM cores use A32/T32 naming (formerly ARM/Thumb), and ARMv8-A A64 instructions are fixed 32-bit with very limited conditional execution. Cortex-M3, M4 and M7 run Thumb-2 only, so startup code and RTOS ports for them are written in Thumb; Cortex-M0 and M0+ run the smaller ARMv6-M Thumb set. Search 'ARMv7-M architecture reference manual', 'Thumb-2 instruction encoding' and 'AAPCS calling convention' to go deeper.
